name: Grammarly
what: A writing assistant that flags spelling and grammar mistakes, suggests tone changes and rewrites sentences. Paid plans add AI text generation, plagiarism checks and AI-text detection.
best_for: Professionals who want cleaner everyday writing across apps
verdict: A dependable safety net for everyday writing, but the free plan caps AI prompts at 100 a month and full rewrites need Pro.

name: Hemingway Editor
what: An editor that highlights hard-to-read and wordy sentences so you can simplify them. The paid Plus version adds AI rewrites, grammar fixes and tone adjustments.
best_for: Writers who want clearer, plainer prose
verdict: Great at pushing you toward simple, readable sentences, but it edits rather than writes, and AI rewrites are capped by plan.

name: Jasper
what: An AI content platform for marketing teams. It keeps output on-brand with saved brand voices and knowledge, and runs agents for common marketing workflows.
best_for: Marketing teams producing on-brand content at volume
verdict: Strong on brand consistency for marketers, but there is no free tier and the price is high for solo writers who just need drafts.

name: Sudowrite
what: An AI writing tool built for fiction. It helps novelists and screenwriters brainstorm, draft, expand and revise scenes while matching their style.
best_for: Novelists and fiction writers
verdict: The most fiction-focused option here, but it runs on monthly credits and the deeper editing features sit in the top plan.

name: Wordtune
what: A writing assistant that offers alternative wordings for your sentences, fixes grammar and summarizes longer texts.
best_for: Rewording and tightening text you already wrote
verdict: Cheap and quick for rewording, but the free plan allows only 10 rewrites a day and it is less suited to drafting from scratch.

name: Claude Code
what: Anthropic's coding agent. It reads your codebase, edits files, runs commands and works with git, from the terminal, IDE, desktop app or web.
best_for: Developers who want an agent to handle multi-step coding tasks
verdict: Handles larger multi-file tasks well, but it needs a paid Claude plan or API usage and plan usage limits apply.

name: Codex
what: OpenAI's coding agent, included with ChatGPT plans. It runs in the ChatGPT apps, a CLI, an IDE extension and in the cloud, where it can take on tasks connected to GitHub, Slack and Linear.
best_for: ChatGPT users who want a coding agent without a separate subscription
verdict: Easy to try since it comes with ChatGPT, including the free plan (desktop app only, still rolling out), but the free tier is meant for quick tasks and serious use needs a paid plan.

name: Cursor
what: An AI coding product with a desktop editor, a command-line tool and cloud agents that work on tasks in parallel. Paid plans bundle Grok AI features.
best_for: Developers who want an AI-first editor with agents built in
verdict: A capable agent-centric editor, but since joining SpaceX its cheapest paid plan ($8 Plus) offers only Grok models, so check plan details if you want other models.

name: GitHub Copilot
what: An AI coding assistant from GitHub that suggests code as you type, answers questions in chat and runs agents that can open pull requests. It works in VS Code, JetBrains, Visual Studio, Xcode, the command line and on GitHub.com.
best_for: Developers already working in GitHub and mainstream IDEs
verdict: The easiest pick if your code lives on GitHub, but the free plan limits chat and agent use, and heavy agent work burns through credits.

name: Recursive Flint
use_cases: keep code on your own machine
what: Flint is an open-weight coding model from Recursive, built for agentic coding on your own hardware. It is a mixture-of-experts model with 40B total parameters, about 2.5B active per token, and runs with tools like llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM and SGLang.
best_for: Developers who want a capable coding model that runs locally and keeps code off third-party servers
verdict: Promising for private, offline coding, but its benchmark results are self-reported, the full weights are about 80 GB, and you have to set up and run the model yourself.

name: Replit
what: A browser-based platform where you describe an app in plain English and its Agent writes the code. Hosting, databases and sign-in come built in.
best_for: Non-developers and makers building working prototypes fast
verdict: The fastest route from idea to live app with no setup, but the free plan publishes only one project and the Agent can make mistakes you must catch.

name: Theorem OSS Verify
use_cases: prove code can't crash on any test input
what: Theorem OSS Verify uses AI to build mathematical proofs, checked by computer, that compiled open source code cannot crash on any input to a given test. Maintainers get the proof plus private reports of any bugs found along the way.
best_for: Maintainers of widely used open source libraries that sit on a security boundary
verdict: Free for accepted open source projects and a stronger guarantee than testing with random inputs, but you have to apply, rebuild your code for one specific processor type (RISC-V), and wait days for each proof.

name: Consensus
what: An AI search engine for peer-reviewed research. It writes answers drawn from papers and shows how much the studies agree on yes/no questions.
best_for: Checking what the science says on a specific question
verdict: Good for a quick read on the evidence behind a claim, though an agreement score can flatten nuance, so read the key studies before you rely on it.

name: Elicit
what: An AI research assistant for academic literature. It searches a large index of papers, summarizes them, lets you chat with them and runs structured review workflows.
best_for: Researchers doing literature or systematic reviews
verdict: Strong for structured literature reviews, but the free tier is limited and the paid plans cost more than most consumer research tools.

name: Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM)
what: Google's research notebook, renamed from NotebookLM in 2026. You add your own sources and it answers questions, writes reports and makes audio overviews based on them.
best_for: Making sense of a pile of your own documents
verdict: Excellent when the answers should come only from sources you supply, but it is less useful for open-ended web research and higher limits require a Google AI subscription.

name: Perplexity
what: An answer engine that searches the web and writes a short answer with inline citations. Paid plans add more advanced models, deeper research runs and more file uploads.
best_for: Fast, cited answers to everyday research questions
verdict: The quickest way to get a sourced answer from the open web, but you still need to click through, since a citation does not guarantee the source says what the summary claims.

name: Semantic Scholar
what: A free search engine for scientific literature from Ai2, the Allen Institute for AI. It covers papers across all fields and offers an AI-assisted reader and a developer API.
best_for: Free, no-signup paper search across all sciences
verdict: A reliable free starting point for finding papers, but it is a search and discovery tool, not one that writes answers or synthesizes findings for you.

name: Adobe Firefly
what: Adobe's AI studio for generating and editing images, video and audio. It offers Adobe's own models alongside a range of third-party models in one place.
best_for: Creatives already working in the Adobe ecosystem
verdict: A sensible choice if you live in Adobe tools, but heavier use runs on a credit system that takes some effort to budget.

name: Canva
what: A browser-based design tool with templates for social posts, slides and print, plus Craft, Canva's own image model, which renders legible text and converts into editable layers. Paid plans add premium content and AI features that share a monthly AI allowance.
best_for: Non-designers who need good-looking graphics fast
verdict: The easiest way for non-designers to produce polished graphics, but its template-first approach can make work look generic, and AI use is capped by plan.

name: Figma Make
use_cases: prototype an app from a prompt
what: Figma's prompt-to-prototype tool. You describe an app or screen, attach designs or files for context, and it builds a working prototype you can then refine on the Figma canvas.
best_for: Product teams prototyping inside Figma
verdict: A natural fit for teams already on Figma, though the free Starter plan's daily AI credits run out quickly on real projects.

name: Ideogram Vector
what: Ideogram Vector creates editable SVG artwork from a text prompt or turns an existing image into a vector. You can recolor, scale and edit individual shapes, in the Ideogram web app or through its API.
best_for: Designers and small teams who need logos, icons or print graphics as clean, scalable vectors
verdict: Saves the manual tracing step for logos and illustrations, but API use is billed per SVG (from $0.10 to vectorize an image) and complex artwork may still need cleanup.

name: Midjourney
what: An image and video generator known for its distinctive, polished visual style. All access is through a paid subscription.
best_for: Striking, stylized images and concept art
verdict: Still a top pick for image quality and style, but there is no free tier, and private generation needs the Pro plan or higher.

name: Recraft
what: An AI image studio aimed at designers. It generates images and editable vector graphics, lets you build reusable custom styles, and gives access to several third-party models.
best_for: Designers who need vector assets and consistent styles
verdict: One of the few generators that outputs real vectors, but free-tier images are public and cannot be used commercially.

name: UseIt Studio
use_cases: turn one design into a matching set
prepare print-ready files with cut lines
what: UseIt Studio is an AI design tool for things you print, cut or fold. You describe changes in plain language, edit text and vector layers, preview the result in 3D, and export print-ready PDF or Illustrator files with cut lines.
best_for: Makers and small sellers designing cards, stickers, packaging or other printed items
verdict: Covers the step most AI image tools skip, getting a design ready for production, but it is early software and its pricing is not published.

name: Descript
use_cases: edit video by editing the transcript
what: Descript is a video and audio editor where you cut and rearrange footage by editing its transcript like a document. It also handles captions, screen recording and remote recording.
best_for: Podcasters and talking-head video creators who would rather edit text than a timeline
verdict: Makes dialogue-heavy edits much faster, but it is less suited to complex visual editing, and free exports are watermarked and capped at 720p.

name: HeyGen
use_cases: translate a video into other languages
make a custom avatar of yourself
what: HeyGen creates videos with AI avatars and voices, including a custom avatar of you. It also translates existing videos into other languages.
best_for: Marketers and creators who want presenter videos or localized versions without a camera
verdict: Useful for avatar and translated videos, but the free plan is limited to three watermarked videos a month of up to one minute each.

name: Pika
use_cases: generate short video clips from prompts
what: Pika is a web app for generating short videos, plus images and audio, from prompts. Paid plans come with monthly credits.
best_for: Hobbyists and social creators who want cheap, quick AI clips
verdict: Paid plans start low, but the free plan includes no monthly credits and no commercial license, so it is more of a trial than a working tier.

name: Runway
what: Runway is a web app that generates video, images and audio from text prompts and reference images. It runs on a monthly credit system.
best_for: Creators and small teams making short generative clips
verdict: A strong pick for generative video, but the free plan is a one-time 125 credits, so real use means a paid plan.

name: Synthesia
use_cases: make training videos with an ai presenter
turn a script into a video
what: Synthesia turns a written script, document or prompt into a video read by an AI avatar. It can also dub existing videos into other languages.
best_for: Companies producing training, onboarding and explainer videos
verdict: Good for fast, consistent presenter videos at scale, but the free plan adds a watermark and does not allow downloads.

name: ElevenLabs
what: ElevenLabs generates lifelike speech from text and can design or clone voices. It also offers transcription, dubbing, sound effects, an API, and Eleven Realtime speech-to-speech models for live voice agents.
best_for: Creators who need high-quality voiceovers and developers building speech features or voice agents
verdict: A leading choice for natural-sounding voices, but credits run out fast on long projects and higher tiers get expensive.

name: Murf AI
use_cases: add text to speech to an app
what: Murf is a voice AI platform with a studio for making voiceovers, AI dubbing for videos, and text-to-speech APIs for developers.
best_for: Teams making narration for training, explainer and marketing videos
verdict: Covers voiceover, dubbing and API needs in one place, but the free plan gives only 10 minutes of generation and no commercial license.

name: Speechify
what: Speechify reads text aloud from web pages, documents and scanned pages on any device. Premium adds natural voices, faster playback, summaries and voice typing.
best_for: Readers who prefer to listen, including people with dyslexia or long reading lists
verdict: Handy for getting through reading by ear, but the free voices sound robotic and Premium is $29 a month on monthly billing.

name: Superwhisper
use_cases: reformat dictation into a set tone
what: Superwhisper turns your speech into text in any app, with modes that shape the output for different tones. It can run models locally and work offline.
best_for: Privacy-minded users who want local, customizable dictation
verdict: Flexible and works offline, but file transcription, translation and cloud AI models need the paid Pro plan.

name: Wispr Flow
use_cases: voice typing on mac and windows
what: Wispr Flow lets you dictate text into any app on Mac, Windows, iPhone and Android. It cleans up your speech into written text as you go.
best_for: People who write a lot and want to type by talking
verdict: Fast for everyday dictation across devices, but the free plan caps desktop dictation at 2,000 words a week.

name: Comet
use_cases: let ai browse websites for you
what: Comet is a web browser from Perplexity with a built-in assistant that can research, compare pages and carry out tasks on websites for you. It runs on Mac, Windows, iOS and Android.
best_for: People who want an AI agent built into their web browser
verdict: A convenient way to hand web chores to an agent, but you must switch browsers and should watch closely when it acts on accounts or purchases.

name: Lindy
what: Lindy is an AI assistant that works inside Slack and your other tools to handle email, scheduling and follow-ups. It asks for approval before taking actions that reach outside, such as sending an email.
best_for: Busy professionals who want an assistant that acts across their apps
verdict: Covers a lot of everyday admin out of the box, but the free credits only last a week and paid use starts near $50 a month.

name: Make
what: Make is a visual automation platform where you map out scenarios that pass data between apps. It adds AI agents and an AI assistant on top of its drag-and-drop builder.
best_for: Visual thinkers building complex, branching automations
verdict: The visual canvas handles complex logic well and the free plan is usable, but credit-based billing makes costs harder to predict, especially with AI steps.

name: n8n
use_cases: connect apis with a visual builder
add human approval to agent actions
what: n8n is a visual workflow builder for automations and AI agents, with the option to drop into code. You can use its cloud service or run the free Community Edition on your own servers.
best_for: Technical teams who want control and self-hosting
verdict: Flexible and cheap to run yourself, but it has a steeper learning curve than Zapier and the cloud plans are priced in euros.

name: Zapier
what: Zapier connects thousands of business apps so work moves between them automatically. Its Agents feature lets you set up AI teammates that act on your data, on command or on a schedule.
best_for: Non-technical teams automating work across many SaaS apps
verdict: The widest app coverage of any automation tool and easy to start, but costs climb quickly once you run many tasks or agent activities.

name: ChatGPT
what: ChatGPT is OpenAI's general AI assistant for writing, questions, analysis and research. Paid plans raise usage limits and add access to more models and tools.
best_for: Anyone who wants one all-round assistant for daily work
verdict: The most widely used all-rounder with a broad feature set, but the free tier is limited and plan names and model options change often.

name: Claude
what: Claude is Anthropic's general AI assistant for writing, analysis and reasoning through problems. It is available free, with paid plans for heavier use.
best_for: Writing-heavy and analytical work
verdict: Strong at careful writing and long documents, but heavy users hit usage limits on lower plans and the top plans cost $100 a month or more.

name: Gemini
use_cases: get help inside gmail and docs
what: Gemini is Google's AI assistant, available as an app and inside Google products. Paid Google AI plans add higher limits, Gemini in Gmail and Docs, and extra Google storage.
best_for: People who already live in Gmail, Docs and Google Drive
verdict: Good value if you already pay for Google storage, but the plan lineup is confusing and the Gmail and Docs features sit behind paid tiers.

name: Microsoft 365 Copilot
what: Microsoft 365 Copilot puts an AI assistant inside Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams for business users. It is sold as an add-on to Microsoft 365 business plans or bundled with them.
best_for: Businesses already running on Microsoft 365
verdict: Fits naturally into Office apps for Microsoft shops, but it is priced per user on top of an existing Microsoft 365 business license.

name: Notion AI
what: Notion AI adds writing help, database autofill and an agent that completes multi-step tasks using your Notion pages, connected apps and the web. It works inside the Notion workspace.
best_for: Teams that already keep their docs and projects in Notion
verdict: Most useful when your work already lives in Notion, but free and Plus plans only get a trial, so the full AI features need the $20 Business plan.

name: Better Analyst
use_cases: schedule data reports to email or slack
what: Better Analyst, formerly Formula Bot, is an AI data analyst that answers plain-English questions about files and connected databases. It builds dashboards and scheduled reports, and shows the SQL or Python behind each answer.
best_for: Non-technical people who need answers and dashboards from their data
verdict: Approachable and transparent about the code it runs, but the free plan's limits are not published and the cheapest paid plan caps you at 2 data sources.

name: Hex
use_cases: write and run sql with ai help
answer data questions in plain english
what: Hex is a data workspace that combines SQL and Python notebooks with an AI agent and shareable data apps. Teams use it to explore warehouse data and publish results for non-technical colleagues.
best_for: Data teams that work in SQL or Python and share analysis with the wider company
verdict: Strong for analysts who already know SQL, but the free plan only gives a trial of the AI agent and paid seats start at $36 per editor a month.

name: Quadratic
use_cases: query a database from a spreadsheet
what: Quadratic is a spreadsheet that runs Python, SQL and JavaScript alongside normal formulas, with an AI assistant built in. It connects to sources like Postgres and QuickBooks.
best_for: Technical users who want code and AI inside a familiar grid
verdict: Flexible if you can read some code, though the free plan has limited AI usage and the extra power can feel like overkill for simple sheets.

name: Rows
use_cases: pull pdf tables into a sheet
what: Rows is an online spreadsheet that connects to other services and lets you ask an AI analyst to work on your data. It can also read PDFs and images and turn them into tables.
best_for: Small teams who want a spreadsheet with built-in data imports and AI help
verdict: A friendly step up from a plain spreadsheet, but the free plan allows only 5 AI tasks a month, so regular AI use means paying.

name: ThoughtSpot
use_cases: search business data in plain english
what: ThoughtSpot is a business intelligence platform where people ask questions of company data in plain language and get charts and dashboards back. Its AI analyst, Spotter, works on top of warehouses like Snowflake and Databricks.
best_for: Companies with a data warehouse that want self-serve BI for business users
verdict: Built for organizations rather than individuals: plans are per user and billed annually, and it needs a data warehouse to be worth it.

name: Fathom
use_cases: sync call notes to a crm
what: Fathom records, transcribes and summarizes your calls, with clips, search and CRM integrations. It can capture meetings with or without a bot joining.
best_for: Individuals and sales teams who want generous free recording
verdict: The free plan includes unlimited recordings and transcripts, which is rare, but advanced AI summaries cover only your first 5 calls a month and bot-free recording is Mac only.

name: Fireflies.ai
use_cases: record zoom, meet and teams calls
send notes to other work tools
what: Fireflies records, transcribes and summarizes your video calls, usually by sending a notetaker bot, or without a bot from its desktop app. It stores meetings as a searchable library and connects to many work apps.
best_for: Teams that want a searchable archive of every meeting
verdict: Covers Zoom, Meet and Teams well and can record without a bot from its desktop app, but the free plan's 400 minutes of storage is a total, not a monthly allowance, so regular use means paying.

name: Granola
use_cases: take meeting notes without a bot
share meeting notes with a team
what: Granola is an AI notepad that captures meeting audio from your device, so no bot joins the call. It combines your own notes with the transcript and lets you chat across past meetings.
best_for: People who take their own notes and dislike meeting bots
verdict: Discreet and pleasant to use, but the free plan keeps only 30 days of meeting history.

name: Otter.ai
what: Otter.ai records and transcribes meetings and conversations, then produces summaries, action items and searchable notes.
best_for: Individuals and teams who want a simple, low-cost meeting transcript
verdict: Easy to start with, but the free plan caps each conversation at 30 minutes and keeps only your 25 most recent ones.

name: tl;dv
what: tl;dv records and transcribes your video meetings, writes notes, and surfaces insights across calls.
best_for: Teams that want recordings plus notes in one place
verdict: A solid all-round recorder with a free plan, but paid plans are priced in euros and cost noticeably more if you pay monthly instead of yearly.
